findings.title: Per-force timing is assigned to this slice by the plan but deferred to 142
findings.description:
The slice plan entry for 141 lists the phase breakdown as "spatial build, spatial query, CSR assembly, **force totals per force**, integration". The design collapses this to a single `force_total_ns` and pushes the per-force breakdown to slice 142.

- **Scope dropped:** this is plan-assigned scope, not an optional extra.
- **Contradicts the slice's own integration criterion:** 142 is the cohesion-only gate and needs that resolution. It would have to extend `PhaseTimings`, the aggregation and the JSON schema (a `schema_version` bump), yet lines 586-588 promise 142 "one file… zero changes elsewhere in the harness".
- **Cheap to fix now:** forces are already called one at a time inside `force_total`. Add `force_breakdown: dict[str, int]` (keyed by workload force name) and its report column to schema v1.

findings.title: Single-name backend registry does not match the per-axis backend selection the plan defines
findings.description:
The plan makes backends selectable per axis: spatial via `spatial.backend` behind `SpatialQuery` (slice 143), forces via engine config behind `BulkForce` (slices 118/144). The harness models one monolithic `backend` name whose runner owns the whole instrumented tick.

- **Slice 143 has no entry point.** It must time `QuadrantsSpatialQuery` against `KDTreeQuery` with unchanged force code. The slice lists 143 in frontmatter `interfaces` but offers it only "may add workloads" (line 527). The numpy runner hardcodes `KDTreeQuery`, and the workload schema has no spatial selector.
- **Slice 144's "single-file" numba backend is not single-file.** `tick_instrumented()` lives in `numpy_backend.py`, so a numba runner must either import from it (meaning it is shared harness code in the wrong place) or become a third copy of the tick body.
- **Slice 142's Metal and CPU-fallback runs are indistinguishable.** Both produce the same `backend`, the same platform tuple and the same `{timestamp}_{workload}_{backend}.json` filename pattern. `platform.processor()` returns only `arm` on Apple Silicon, so the chip model is not captured either.

Suggested fix, without adding mechanism:
- Put the instrumented CPU tick in a shared module (for example `bench/instrumented_tick.py`) that takes the `SpatialQuery` and force list as parameters.
- Let a registered backend be a named (spatial, forces, device) composition.
- Add a `device`/variant field to the JSON header and the filename.

findings.title: `tick_instrumented()` duplicates the tick body, and the document contradicts itself about calling `tick()`
findings.description:
Lines 131-132 and 541 say the NumPy runner "calls `tick()` directly". Decision B (lines 255-267) and lines 498-501 say it runs a parallel re-implementation of the tick body. Only one can be true, and per-phase brackets cannot be obtained by calling `tick()`.

Consequences of the re-implementation as designed:
- **The harness benchmarks a copy, not the production path.** The architecture's "profile before/after" principle is about the production tick.
- **The copy depends on engine internals.** Phase helpers and per-tick profile-array setup are not part of slice 140's contract, and this is not listed under "Interfaces Required" (a hidden dependency).
- **Phase-boundary drift is admitted to be undetectable** (lines 691-695). The bit-equality test catches algorithmic drift only.
- **It conflicts with the project's DRY rule**, and the "~5 lines per phase" estimate counts the timer brackets, not the duplicated tick logic.

At minimum:
- Resolve the contradiction and list the engine internals the copy consumes.
- Add a cheap guard: time uninstrumented `tick()` over the same workload and report (or assert a bound on) the gap against `total_ns`. This also quantifies the observer effect.
- Reconsider rejected option A in its lightest form: an optional phase-callback argument defaulting to none. The design rejects it on a "third call site" threshold while accepting a permanently hand-synced copy.

findings.title: SHA-256 parity hash cannot serve the consumers it is promised to
findings.description:
The design says downstream consumers will interpret the hash "within the documented tolerance band" and that slice 145's tick-level parity test uses the NumPy hash as reference (lines 533-534). A cryptographic hash supports only exact equality.

- **Slice 145 needs tolerance, not equality.** The plan defines its parity as "within a documented tolerance for non-deterministic GPU reductions", and the plan's open questions confirm GPU reduction order is not deterministic.
- **Numba is unlikely to be bit-identical either**, since its explicit per-edge loops accumulate in a different order than NumPy's `reduceat`.
- **So the hash proves only same-backend run-to-run determinism.** The plan entry for 141 does not ask for that, and the slice's own Open Questions already name `tools/run_deterministic_trajectory.py` (slice 140) as "the parity oracle".

Either cut `parity.py`, the hash field and its tests, or have the harness dump final positions/velocities (`.npz`) so a consumer can run `allclose` against the NumPy reference. In both cases remove the "Provides to 145" claim as written.

Smaller inconsistency: line 81 says the hash is taken "post-warmup", line 460 says "after the measure phase".

findings.title: Reproducibility metadata and non-YAML I/O paths have unspecified failure handling
findings.description:
The Value section and line 185 promise runs "reproducible by repo hash + workload name". The failure-mode list covers YAML loading, registry lookup and `setup`, but not the paths that claim rests on.

- **`git rev-parse HEAD` failure is not handled.** Git may be absent, or the tree may be an exported copy. Per "no silent fallbacks", state fail or an explicit placeholder.
- **A dirty working tree is not recorded.** Benchmarks are typically run on uncommitted optimization work, so a bare SHA will often misattribute numbers. Add a `git_dirty` flag.
- **`tick_once` raising mid-measure is not specified.** State whether a partial report is written (recommend none, non-zero exit, `finalize` still called).
- **`bench/results/` missing or unwritable is not specified.**
- **Dependency versions are missing from the header.** `numpy` now, and `numba`/`quadrants` later, materially change timings and are needed for the "re-run last quarter's bench" claim.

findings.title: A few items can be cut or simplified
findings.description:
Overall weight is reasonable for the plan's 3/5 effort; the registry and three workloads are justified by "Numba and Quadrants slot in". Items nothing uses yet:
- `--all-backends` with one registered backend.
- `--workload-dir`.
- The "old readers must reject unknown versions" rule, when no reader exists.
- Using `pytest-benchmark` for stub-backend tests that assert arithmetic on synthetic timings (plain pytest suffices).

Separately, `--list-backends` and `--list-workloads` appear only in the Verification Walkthrough and should be added to the CLI section or dropped.

findings.title: Internal inconsistencies to clean up before task breakdown
findings.description:
- **Workload fields:** Scope (lines 70-72) lists `density`, "formation seed" and "RNG seed". The schema has no density field and a single `seed`.
- **Unspecified workloads:** `dispersed` and `packed-herd` have no N or geometry given, though they are the formation regimes the plan names.
- **JSON shape:** Scope says "one record per (workload, backend, phase)". The schema is one file per (workload, backend) with nested phases.
- **Markdown report:** "sortable on TPS" has no meaning for a static table, and "one table per workload across all backends in `bench/results/`" does not say which of several timestamped runs per backend is used.
- **Spatial module path:** `migratory.spatial` (line 136) versus `engine.spatial.KDTreeQuery` (line 542).
- **Phase naming:** the design says its phase names "correspond exactly" to the architecture's budget table, but the architecture calls the CSR phase `self_excl_cap`. Note the rename.
- **Walkthrough step 9:** the architecture's `force_total` figure is for 4 forces at N=2,492, while `mid-flock` engages 5 forces at N=3,500. Say so, so the shape comparison is not misread.

findings.title: Dependency direction and layer boundaries
findings.description: `bench` depends on `engine` and never the reverse. The world server, websocket layer and logging-sim are excluded, consistent with "the wire is a separate problem". `TickResult` (slice 140) is the only cross-backend data contract consumed, and no changes to `src/migratory/engine/` or `src/migratory_server/` are permitted by the success criteria.

findings.title: Scope deferrals consistent with the plan
findings.description:
- **Backends:** NumPy-only at first matches "Standalone against NumPy at first; Numba and Quadrants slot in".
- **Platforms:** deferring the CUDA run and a CI matrix is consistent with Apple Silicon as the primary development platform.
- **Output:** JSON plus a Markdown summary satisfies "machine-readable (CSV/JSON)… plus a human-readable summary".
- **Formation breakdown:** per-workload tables over the three named regimes provide the formation-dependent breakdown.
- **Other exclusions:** regression gating, memory measurement and charting are correctly out of scope.
- **NFR:** none from the architecture applies to the harness path itself.
